props.title: Take Care of My Cat

sections.content: **Take Care of My Cat** (2001) masterfully captures the fragmenting friendships of five young Korean women after high school, setting a new standard for intimate coming-of-age dramas. Director Jeong Jae-eun's debut feature anticipated the sensitive portrayals of female friendship that would later emerge in films like **Frances Ha** (2012) and **Our Little Sister** (2015). Through innovative use of text messages on screen and urban cinematography, the film documents the economic and social pressures facing young women in rapidly modernizing South Korea, predating similar themes in **Burning** (2018) and House of Hummingbird (2018).

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a crucial period for Korean cinema's exploration of female friendship and urban alienation. While **Take Care of My Cat** (2001) took an intimate approach, films like **My Sassy Girl** (2001) and **Linda Linda Linda** (2005) offered different perspectives on young women's experiences in East Asian metropolises. The economic anxiety depicted through Hae-joo's office job and Ji-young's artistic aspirations eerily foreshadowed themes that would become central to contemporary Korean cinema, culminating in works like **Parasite** (2019).

The film's innovative visual style, particularly its use of mobile phone text messages as both communication and artistic elements, established a visual language for depicting digital interaction that influenced later works like **Personal Shopper** (2016) and **Searching** (2018). The roaming cat that connects the characters serves as both a literal plot device and a metaphor for the characters' drifting relationships, a technique that would be echoed in films like **Still Walking** (2008). sections.content: Following **Take Care of My Cat** (2001), a new wave of Asian films began exploring female friendship with greater nuance. Works like **Our Times** (2015) and **Girls Always Happy** (2018) built upon its foundation, examining how economic pressures and social expectations shape women's relationships. The film's influence extends to recent works like **Better Days** (2019), which similarly explores young women's struggles within oppressive social structures.
